# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
This is a strong follow-up, and it resolves most of the questions the earlier documents left open:

- It adds log-based hours as a second check on timesheets.
- It registers the mediation test before the outcome data existed.
- It reports the counter arm's termination with control-office comparisons, which the nine-month report lacked.
- It correctly diagnoses the meta-analysis's duration evidence: all four long studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours.
- It is candid about the Halden survivors and the unplanned meeting audit.

The body is mostly well calibrated. The Summary overstates in three places, and there are some substantive issues with the mediation analysis and the decay estimate.

## Arithmetic

| Quantity | Check |
|---|---|
| Output per hour, timesheets, 24 months | 0.966 / 0.88 → +9.8% ✓ |
| Output per hour, logs, 24 months | 0.966 / 0.89 → +8.5% ✓ |
| Decline in per-hour gain, timesheets | 12.5 → 9.8 = −22%, "about a quarter" ✓ |
| Halden hours ratio | 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866 (−13.4%) ✓ |
| Halden per-hour gain | 96.8 / 86.6 → +11.8% ✓ |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 = 100 ✓ |

## 1. The Summary overstates in ways the body doesn't

**It compares across different measures.** The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months."
- 12.5% is based on timesheets; 8.5% is based on system logs.
- The like-for-like decline is 12.5 → 9.8 (about −22%), not 12.5 → 8.5 (−32%).
- The body gets this right ("on the like-for-like timesheet measure"). The Summary should match it.

**"Confirms" overstates the mediation result.** The Summary says the mediation test "confirms" that meetings account for 47%.
- Mediation estimates rest on sequential ignorability, which the Limitations rightly say a cluster trial can't guarantee.
- "Supports" or "is consistent with" would be accurate.

**It reframes one of the reversions.** The Summary says all three reverting organisations had "client-facing or coverage obligations."
- That holds for the hospitality group and the retail chain.
- The marketing agency reverted over *client deadlines*. That is discretionary work, as the meta-analysis coded it.
- Grouping it under "client-facing" hides the fact that one reversion came from the kind of work where reduced hours are supposed to suit best.

## 2. The decay estimate is probably confounded by the control-office meeting audit

The paper treats the month-15 meeting audit in two control offices as a side observation. It also affects the main estimate.

**It biases the estimate towards zero.**
- Two of the seven control offices raised output per hour by about 4.1% after cutting meetings.
- That lifts the control mean by roughly 1.2 percentage points (2/7 × 4.1).
- In a difference-in-differences design, that lowers the measured treatment effect.

**It could explain much of the decline.**
- Up to about 1.2 of the 2.7-point drop in the timesheet estimate could reflect controls improving, not treated offices fading.
- "Consistent with some fading of an initial effect" is still fair, but the paper should report a sensitivity analysis that excludes the two audited offices or the post-audit months.

**The control meeting figures don't obviously reconcile.**
- Control meeting time is reported as 7.2 → 7.0 hours overall.
- If two of seven offices fell by 2.1 hours each, that alone would lower the control average by about 0.6 hours.
- For the overall average to fall only 0.2 hours, the other five offices must have *increased* meeting time by about 0.5 hours each, or the audited offices drifted back by month 24.
- Either is possible, but it needs stating.

## 3. Questions about the mediation analysis

**What do the log hours measure?**
- Logs record "active log-in time on the case-management system", which presumably excludes meetings.
- If so, cutting meetings doesn't directly change output per *log* hour: freed time moves into case work, raising both output and log hours.
- In that case the meetings pathway must work through something like less fragmentation or better focus, not by removing low-value time.
- That is a different mechanism from the one the paper describes ("removing low-value time").
- The definition also matters for the claim that logs show "more work" than timesheets. Logs fall less partly because meeting time has moved into logged case work.

**Where did the baseline meeting data come from?**
- The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six, with no pre-period.
- This report gives baseline figures (7.4 and 7.2 hours).
- If these were recovered retrospectively from calendar histories, say so. That is fine, but it is a change in method.

**How many independent units are there?**
- "A larger sample of office-months" adds observations, but office-months within an office aren't independent.
- The effective sample is still 7 treated and 7 control offices.
- A CI of 28–66% looks narrow for 14 clusters. The paper should say how clustering was handled, for example by cluster bootstrap.

**The test isn't an independent replication.**
- Registering at month 11 makes the analysis confirmatory in the procedural sense.
- But the hypothesis came from these same seven offices, and the month-6 data overlap with the mediator series.
- That is weaker than testing on new offices. This partly answers the Comment's "seven offices" objection rather than refuting it.

**Can the shares be added?**
- Fewer meetings may reduce fatigue, so the two pathways may not be separable.
- The paper should state whether the shares come from a joint model with the mediators allowed to correlate.
- If the meetings effect runs partly through fatigue, the 47/18 split depends on the model chosen.

## 4. The backlog question is still unanswered

The nine-month limitations flagged whether "backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines." That question is now more pressing:

- Output per FTE has stayed below control for two years (−3.4%).
- Unless demand also fell, that implies a growing queue.

The report should give backlog size, case age, and the share of cases exceeding statutory deadlines by arm.

The appeal overturn rate (3.2% vs 3.0%) can now finally capture treated-period decisions, which is useful. It still needs a confidence interval.

## 5. Halden follow-up: "upper bound" is the wrong term

The caveats are good ("survivors twice over"). But the 11 organisations have no comparison group, and their output is measured against a baseline more than two years old.

- Business growth, staff changes or market conditions over that period could push the figure either way.
- So it is *likely upward-biased* for the reasons given, but it isn't an *upper bound* in any formal sense.

**Non-response.** Only 14 of 23 organisations responded. If the nine non-responders included further reversions, the reversion rate (3/14) is understated.

**The rising estimate.** The Halden estimate rises from 10.8% to 11.8% while Varden's falls. That divergence is itself consistent with the selection the authors describe and could be noted.

## 6. Smaller points

**Sick days.**
- They are still reported per FTE (−27%) without adjusting for fewer scheduled days.
- If treated staff work four days, a large part of the fall is mechanical.
- This was raised for the nine-month report and remains unaddressed.

**Resignations.** No confidence intervals are given.

**The counter-arm cost estimate.**
- 12% more staff at unchanged pay suggests a rise in cost per contact closer to 12% than 9%.
- The 9% presumably assumes non-labour costs, or recovered abandoned contacts. State which.
- 12% also roughly matches restoring *throughput* (1/0.886 ≈ 1.13). Restoring staff *presence*, which is what drives waiting times, would take closer to 20% (1/0.83).
- Was 12% judged sufficient to restore waits?

**Authorship and tone.**
- R. Okafor is an author of the Halden pilot and co-reports its follow-up.
- The Varden authors are adjudicating criticism of their own exploratory analysis.
- Neither is a problem in itself, and the body is fair. But phrasing like "since dismissed as post hoc" reads as score-settling. A neutral restatement would sit better alongside a conflict-of-interest note.

## Bearing on the earlier claims

On the evidence here:

- **The Comment's "entirely an artifact":** contradicted. A randomised comparison with record-based output and log-measured hours finds +8.5% (3.4 to 13.8) at 24 months. The paper is right to give the Comment credit for the measurement problems it identified.
- **The meta-analysis's "no sign of decay":** contradicted for the one controlled long-follow-up study. The size of the decay is uncertain, given the contamination in point 2.
- **The meetings mechanism:** supported more strongly than before, with the identification caveats above. The unplanned audit raises the right next question: can reorganising work without cutting hours capture much of the gain? Only a trial with a reorganise-only arm can answer that.
- **Coverage-bound work:** settled for practical purposes in this setting. The county judged it not viable without more staff.

The fitting closing point for the series is that this last report is well calibrated in its body but drifts towards overstatement in its Summary, which is the part most readers will quote.
